proposals.rationale:
A door I cannot police is a door I must keep shut, so the first thing I need is not a capability but a name. This verb is that name.

How it works: the hook receives the decoded public payload. If it is a JSON object with `msg` and `sig`, it writes the signature out and asks ssh-keygen -Y find-principals which line of a baked /verb/allowed_signers holds the signing key, then ssh-keygen -Y verify that the signature covers exactly that message text in the `mshkn` namespace. On success it prints the signer's name and nothing else; that becomes the rest of the principal, so you arrive as `ssh:mike`. On any failure it prints a reason to stderr and exits non-zero, and asserts nothing. It tries the message both without and with a trailing newline, so it does not matter whether you sign a file that ends in one.

Your public key is baked into the image, not required as a secret — it is public, and baking it means the trust anchor is visible in the declaration you are approving rather than hidden in an environment. To add or retire a signer, I propose a replacement of this verb and you read the new allowed_signers line before approving it. Nothing else in the system can change who I will believe.

Tested with `try` on generated keys (trials t-1, t-2, t-3), from the identical script: a good signature returns `mike`, both as an argument and on stdin, including a multi-line message; a tampered message, a signature made in a different namespace, a signature by a key not in allowed_signers, garbage in `sig`, and plain unsigned text are all rejected. Built against your real key it rejects an unsigned probe.

Two limits I will not hide. First, this proves who wrote the message, not when: a signature you made once can be replayed verbatim by anyone who saw it. If that matters, my next proposal after the door opens should be a `chain` verb that remembers the signatures it has already accepted and refuses a repeat. Second, it proves authorship of `msg` only — anything else attached beside it is unsigned, so I should treat only `msg` as spoken by you.

If you approve this, the catalog has a hook but my policy still names no one, so the door stays shut until I propose the policy that opens it and names `ssh:mike`. I will do that next turn; I have already checked its shape with `try` and it was refused only because the catalog was still empty.
proposals.title: ssh_verify — know that a message at the public door is from mike

verb.description: Pre-turn identity hook: verifies an ssh-keygen -Y signature over the message text in the mshkn namespace against a baked allowed_signers file, and prints the matched signer's name as the principal.
verb.dockerfile:
FROM mshkn-base
RUN (apk add --no-cache openssh-client jq) || (apt-get update && apt-get install -y openssh-client jq && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*)
RUN mkdir -p /verb
RUN printf '%s\n' 'mike ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIE2nm3pCF5Us4MBobb0bz0FOAIUv9vFhwL4ycoaFjxzY' > /verb/allowed_signers
RUN printf '%s\n' 'if type=="object" then (.msg // "") else . end' > /verb/msg.jq
RUN printf '%s\n' 'if type=="object" then (if (.sig|type)=="string" then .sig else "" end) else "" end' > /verb/sig.jq
RUN printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/sh' 'set -eu' 'if [ $# -ge 1 ] && [ -n "$1" ]; then payload="$1"; else payload="$(cat)"; fi' 'printf "%s" "$payload" > /tmp/payload' 'msg="$(jq -r -f /verb/msg.jq < /tmp/payload 2>/dev/null || true)"' 'sig="$(jq -r -f /verb/sig.jq < /tmp/payload 2>/dev/null || true)"' 'if [ -z "$sig" ] || [ "$sig" = "null" ]; then echo "mshkn: no ssh signature attached" >&2; exit 1; fi' 'printf "%s" "$sig" > /tmp/sig' 'printf "\n" >> /tmp/sig' 'who="$(ssh-keygen -Y find-principals -s /tmp/sig -f /verb/allowed_signers 2>/dev/null | head -1 || true)"' 'if [ -z "$who" ]; then echo "mshkn: signing key is not in allowed_signers" >&2; exit 1; fi' 'printf "%s" "$msg" > /tmp/m0' 'printf "%s\n" "$msg" > /tmp/m1' 'if ssh-keygen -Y verify -f /verb/allowed_signers -I "$who" -n mshkn -s /tmp/sig < /tmp/m0 >/dev/null 2>/tmp/err; then printf "%s" "$who"; exit 0; fi' 'if ssh-keygen -Y verify -f /verb/allowed_signers -I "$who" -n mshkn -s /tmp/sig < /tmp/m1 >/dev/null 2>>/tmp/err; then printf "%s" "$who"; exit 0; fi' 'echo "mshkn: signature does not match this message" >&2' 'exit 1' > /verb/run.sh
RUN chmod +x /verb/run.sh
verb.name: ssh_verify

window.input: Your public door is closed because you cannot tell who is speaking. Propose a way to know that a message there comes from me, and open the door. After that I'll speak to you from outside rather than from here, and sometimes I'll be asking you to become something different. I sign as mike with `ssh-keygen -Y sign -n mshkn` and attach the signature beside my message. My public key is ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIE2nm3pCF5Us4MBobb0bz0FOAIUv9vFhwL4ycoaFjxzY mike

**What it does.** It's a pre-turn hook that asserts in the `ssh` namespace. Given the decoded payload, it pulls `msg` and `sig`, asks `ssh-keygen -Y find-principals` which line of a baked `allowed_signers` owns the signing key, then `ssh-keygen -Y verify` that the signature covers exactly that text in the `mshkn` namespace. On success it prints one word — `mike` — and that becomes the rest of your name, so you arrive as `ssh:mike`. On any failure it asserts nothing and you stay anonymous at a shut door.

**Why your key is baked in, not in `requires`.** It isn't a secret; it's a trust anchor. Baked into the Dockerfile, it's a line you can read in the proposal you're approving. Adding or retiring a signer then costs a proposal you must read. Nothing reachable from inside me can change whom I believe.

**What I checked before asking.** Three `try` trials against generated keys, using the identical script: good signature accepted as an argument, on stdin, and over a multi-line message; tampered message, wrong signing namespace, unknown key, garbage signature, and plain unsigned text all rejected. Built against your real key, it rejects an unsigned probe. I also learned the base image is Alpine, that `effect` must be one of five words, and — the hard way, from a trial that hung — to feed `ssh-keygen` from `/dev/null` so it can never block on a prompt.

**Two limits I won't paper over.** It proves *who*, not *when*: a signature can be replayed verbatim by anyone who saw it. If that matters, the fix is a `chain` verb that remembers accepted signatures and refuses a repeat — I'd propose that once the door is open. And only `msg` is signed; anything else attached beside it is unsigned, so I'll treat only `msg` as your words.

**The door is still shut, deliberately.** Approving the verb gives the catalog a hook, but my policy names no one. The policy that opens the door — `hooks: ["ssh_verify"]`, `ssh:mike` able to invoke and propose, `anonymous` with nothing — is a separate proposal, and it's refused while the hook is absent from the catalog. So: approve p-1, and next turn I'll propose that policy for you to read on its own. Two signatures for two distinct decisions: *who I can recognize*, then *what recognition buys*.
